title: Part-time o fixed-term worker ka? New equal-treatment rules started October 1
summary: From October 1, 2026, Japan changed rules for part-time and fixed-term workers. Employers must tell covered workers at hiring or contract renewal that they can ask for an explanation of differences in treatment versus regular workers, while revised equal-pay guidance clarifies bonuses, retirement allowances, allowances and benefits.
why_it_matters: Kung part-time, arubaito, or fixed-term/contract worker ka, may mas malinaw ka nang basis to review pay, allowances, leave and benefits and ask your employer to explain specific differences. A difference is not automatically illegal; the law targets unreasonable differences and, in some cases, discriminatory treatment.

claims.text: The revised rules took effect on October 1, 2026 and cover added hiring disclosures, revisions to the equal-pay/equal-treatment guideline, and changes to employment-management measures.
claims.basis: MHLW and Labour Bureau implementation guidance

claims.text: When hiring a part-time or fixed-term worker, including at contract renewal, the employer must now state that the worker can request an explanation of the content and reasons for treatment differences versus regular workers.
claims.basis: MHLW explanation of the added disclosure item

claims.text: If a part-time or fixed-term worker asks, the employer must explain the content and reasons for treatment differences and the matters considered when determining the worker's treatment.
claims.basis: Part-Time and Fixed-Term Employment Act Article 14(2) guidance

claims.text: The revised guideline clarifies treatment of bonuses, retirement allowances, various allowances and welfare benefits based on court decisions and other developments.
claims.basis: MHLW summary of the revised equal-pay guideline

claims.text: MHLW gives family allowance as an example: where a part-time or fixed-term worker is expected to work for a correspondingly continuous period, the guideline says the same allowance should be paid as to a regular worker.
claims.basis: MHLW example under the revised guideline

claims.text: Workers who notice a specific difference in pay, allowances, leave or benefits have a practical reason to document that difference and ask for an explanation, but the existence of a difference alone does not prove that it is unlawful or create an automatic entitlement to back pay.
claims.basis: Inference from the law's unreasonable-difference standard and explanation mechanism

content.key_message: Part-time, arubaito, o fixed-term/contract worker ka? Since October 1, mas malinaw na ang right mo to know that you can ask why your treatment differs from a regular worker. Check your contract, payslips, allowances, leave and benefits, then ask about a specific difference if something does not line up.
content.who_is_affected: People in Japan working as part-time workers or on fixed-term employment contracts, especially those comparing their pay, allowances, leave or benefits with regular workers in the same company.
content.when: The revised rules took effect on October 1, 2026.
content.financial_impact: No universal yen amount applies. The practical impact depends on the worker's actual treatment and whether a particular difference is justified under the law and revised guideline.
content.risk_if_ignored: You may miss a chance to identify and clarify an unexplained treatment difference. But assuming every difference is illegal can also lead to incorrect expectations.
content.deadline: No general worker filing deadline is stated in the cited October 1 guidance. The rule is already in effect.
content.effort: Low to medium: gather your contract and recent payslips, compare specific treatment items, then ask HR/employer for an explanation where needed.
content.potential_benefit: A clearer explanation of your treatment and, where a company identifies an unreasonable difference, a basis for correcting employment practices.
content.downside: The revised rule does not guarantee that every difference will be removed; lawful differences can depend on job content, responsibility, transfer scope and other relevant circumstances.
content.what_would_change_mind: Later MHLW guidance, court decisions or statutory amendments that materially change the explanation duty or treatment standards.
what_to_do_now: Get your current employment contract or 労働条件通知書 and recent payslips.
List specific items you want to compare: base pay, bonus, retirement allowance, family/housing allowances, leave, training or welfare benefits.
If you were hired or renewed from October 1 onward, check whether your employment documents say you can request an explanation of treatment differences.
For a specific difference, ask HR/employer what the difference is and why it applies to your role. Keep the written reply or dated notes.
If the explanation remains unclear, use the employment-environment/equal-opportunity consultation section of your prefectural Labour Bureau rather than relying only on social-media advice.
prepare: Employment contract or 労働条件通知書
Recent payslips and any bonus/allowance statements
Work rules or benefit descriptions you can access
A short factual list of the exact treatment differences you want explained
avoid: Do not assume that every difference between a regular and non-regular worker is automatically illegal.
Do not compare only job titles; actual duties, responsibility, transfer scope and other circumstances can matter.
Do not rely on verbal memory alone when asking about a potentially important pay or benefit difference; keep documents and dated notes.
content.watch: Watch for updated MHLW examples, Labour Bureau guidance and court decisions applying the revised guideline to specific allowances and benefits.
content.bottom_line: FACT: Japan's revised part-time/fixed-term rules have applied since October 1, 2026, including a new hiring/renewal disclosure that workers can ask for explanations of treatment differences and revised equal-treatment guidance. INFERENCE: if you see a concrete difference in pay, allowances, leave or benefits, document it and ask why—but do not assume the difference is automatically unlawful.
